# A certificate-free improvement of the upper bound for transversals of (7,2)-hypergraphs

*[Author names to be added]* — Draft, 23 September 2026. Not submitted; not for distribution.

*Plain-text mirror of `paper_0865.tex` (generated by `w5_paper_tex2md.py`; the LaTeX file is authoritative).*
## Abstract

Let $f(k,7)$ be the largest transversal number of a $k$-uniform hypergraph in which every at most seven edges can be met by two points. Fon-Der-Flaass, Kostochka and Woodall proved $\lceil 3k/4\rceil \le f(k,7)\le\lceil 7k/8\rceil $, and Erdős asked whether $f(k,7)=(3/4+o(1))k$; the question (Erdős Problem #644) is open. We prove

$$
f(k,7)\le\lceil 173k/200\rceil +10\qquad(k\ge1000),
$$

so $\limsup_k f(k,7)/k\le 0.865<7/8$. The proof is entirely by hand. Its core is a local closing lemma (Proposition 4.1) for a good triple whose largest pair intersection is at most $23k/50$; it is proved by an eight-case analysis that uses three adaptive request lemmas, the static construction of [FKW, Lemma 1, Case 2], and two further static request templates with closed-form budgets. A maximality argument and two intersection-gap lemmas complete the proof. We also record, separately from the main theorem, several structural lemmas (a sharp span bound for good triples, a two-colour lemma, a $K_4$ criterion and a spread lemma) as tools toward the $3/4$ question. Independent computer checks are described in an appendix; the proof does not depend on them.

*Status of this draft.* This manuscript was prepared with AI assistance. Several lemmas are re-derivations, in uniform notation and with complete proofs, of lemmas from an unpublished working note (see Remark 1.3). Nothing here has been refereed externally.

## 1. Introduction

A *transversal* of a family of sets is a set meeting every member; $\tau(\mathcal H)$ denotes the minimum size of a transversal of $\mathcal H$. For integers $p>t\ge1$ and $k\ge2$, say that $\mathcal H$ has *property $(p,t)$* if every subfamily of at most $p$ edges has a transversal of size at most $t$. Erdős, Hajnal and Tuza [EHT] raised the problem of determining the largest value $f(k,p,t)$ of $\tau(\mathcal H)$ over $k$-uniform families $\mathcal H$ with property $(p,t)$ (as reported in [FKW]). We write $f(k,p)=f(k,p,2)$. (In [FKW] the property is stated for subfamilies of exactly $p$ edges; for families with at least $p$ edges the two versions coincide, and families with at most six edges have $\tau\le6$, which is irrelevant for the asymptotic questions below.) The same parameter is studied in the notation $h_r(k,\ell)$ by Bucić, Korándi and Sudakov [BKS], who survey its history.

Erdős, Fon-Der-Flaass, Kostochka and Tuza [EFKT] determined $f(k,p)$ for $3\le p\le6$; in particular $f(k,6)=k$, and for these $p$ the extremal families are the largest complete $k$-uniform hypergraphs with property $(p,2)$ (both statements as reported in [FKW]). The explicit values $f(k,3)=2k$, $f(k,4)=\lfloor 3k/2\rfloor $ and $f(k,5)=\lfloor 5k/4\rfloor $ are recorded in our sources only at second hand [citation to check]. For $p=7$, Fon-Der-Flaass, Kostochka and Woodall [FKW] proved

$$
f(k,7)\le\lceil 7k/8\rceil \qquad(k\ge8),
$$

and showed that complete hypergraphs are no longer extremal: for $m\ge10$ (and, by their remark, already for $m\ge4$) the family of all $4m$-subsets of a $(7m+1)$-set that meet a fixed $4m$-set in an odd number of points has property $(7,2)$ and transversal number $3m+1$, whereas every complete $4m$-uniform hypergraph with property $(7,2)$ has transversal number at most $3m$. Complete hypergraphs give $f(k,7)\ge\lceil 3k/4\rceil $ (Proposition 2.8). Erdős asked whether

$$
f(k,7)=\Bigl(\tfrac34+o(1)\Bigr)k ;
$$

the paper [FKW] describes itself as partially answering a question of [EFKT], and the question is listed as Problem #644 on the Erdős problems website [EP], where it is marked open. The best published bounds we know of are therefore $3/4\le\liminf f(k,7)/k\le\limsup f(k,7)/k\le7/8$. We have not been able to consult [Kos], which treats property $(p,2)$ for large $p$; the Erdős problems page [EP] lists no improvement for $p=7$ [literature search not exhaustive].

**Theorem 1.1.** For every integer $k\ge1000$,

$$
f(k,7)\le\lceil 173k/200\rceil +10 .
$$

In particular $\limsup_{k\to\infty}f(k,7)/k\le173/200=0.865<7/8$. By Lemma 2.7 the same bound holds for families of rank at most $k$.

**Remark 1.2 (What is proved by hand).** Every step of the proof of Theorem 1.1 is a finite chain of explicit inequalities between linear expressions in the parameters; no computer search, linear-programming certificate or case enumeration by machine is used. The appendix lists independent exact computer checks, which are a sanity supplement only.

**Remark 1.3 (Provenance).** The coefficient $173/200$, the constants $h=23/50$ and $\ell=43/200$, and Lemmas 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3 below come from an unpublished, computer-assisted working note (Lemmas 7.18, 7.26, 7.32, 7.31, 7.27, 7.41 and 7.50 there). In that note the bound $\lceil 173k/200\rceil +10$ relied on an exact finite certificate (11940 tetrahedral proof nodes) for the exclusion of pair intersections in $[27k/100,23k/50]$; the note also reports stronger computer-assisted coefficients (down to $6/7$), which have not been independently reviewed and are not used here. The new ingredients of the present paper are Proposition 4.1, which replaces that certificate by an eight-case hand argument, the closed-form budgets of the static templates in Lemmas 3.5 and 3.6 (whose label patterns occur among the machine-enumerated templates of the note), and the organisation of the proof around a maximality threshold at $23k/50$. Lemma 3.1 is a parametrised form of Case 2 of [FKW, Lemma 1].

### Strategy

Let $r=k$, $\beta=173/200$, and suppose an $r$-uniform family with property $(7,2)$ has $\tau>K:=\lceil \beta r\rceil +10$. Following [FKW], we build bad subfamilies of at most seven edges from a *good triple* (three edges with no common point) by *requests*: since $\tau>K$, every set of at most $K$ points is avoided by some edge. Let $m$ be the largest pair intersection not exceeding $\lfloor 23r/50\rfloor $. A balanced request produces a good triple with intersections $m\ge y\ge z$ and $m+2y\le227r/200$ (the maximality of $m$ gives $y,z\le m$). Proposition 4.1 closes every such triple unless $m<43r/200$. Hence there is no pair intersection in $[43r/200,23r/50]$. Lemma 5.1 extends the gap up to $r/2$, and then the conditional finishing Lemma 5.3 gives $\tau\le\lceil \beta r\rceil +4$, a contradiction.

Section 2 collects preliminaries, Section 3 the closing lemmas for good triples, Section 4 the local Proposition, Section 5 the gap lemmas and Section 6 the proof of Theorem 1.1. Section 7, which is logically independent of the main theorem, records structural lemmas aimed at the $3/4$ question. Appendix A describes computer checks.

## 2. Preliminaries

A *family* (hypergraph) $\mathcal H$ is a finite collection of finite nonempty sets (edges) on a vertex set $V$; it is *$r$-uniform* if all edges have $r$ points and has *rank at most $k$* if all edges have at most $k$ points. A *bad subfamily* is a set of at most seven edges without a transversal of size at most $2$; thus $\mathcal H$ has property $(7,2)$ if and only if it has no bad subfamily. A *pair intersection* is $|E\cap F|$ for distinct edges $E,F$. For sets $E_1,\dots,E_j$ and a point $v$ let $\sigma(v)=\{i:v\in E_i\}$.

**Lemma 2.1 (requests).** If $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$ and $|D|\le T$, then some edge of $\mathcal H$ is disjoint from $D$.

*Proof.* Otherwise $D$ is a transversal of size at most $T$.
 ∎

We call this *requesting an edge avoiding $D$*; the edge is the *response*. Requests may depend on earlier responses.

**Lemma 2.2 (closing principle).** Let $E_1,\dots,E_j$ be edges with $E_1\cap\dots\cap E_j=\emptyset$, and let $D_1,\dots,D_s$, $j+s\le7$, be sets such that every $2$-set $\{p,q\}$ with $\sigma(p)\cup\sigma(q)=\{1,\dots,j\}$ is contained in some $D_i$. If $H_i$ is an edge disjoint from $D_i$ ($1\le i\le s$), then $\{E_1,\dots,E_j,H_1,\dots,H_s\}$ is a bad subfamily.

*Proof.* A transversal $\{p,q\}$ of size at most two ($p=q$ allowed) of $E_1,\dots,E_j$ satisfies $\sigma(p)\cup\sigma(q)=\{1,\dots,j\}$, and $p\ne q$ since no point lies in all $E_i$. So $\{p,q\}\subseteq D_i$ for some $i$ and $H_i$ misses both points. The subfamily has at most seven distinct members; coincidences among the edges only make it smaller.
 ∎

**Lemma 2.3 (candidate pairs of a good triple).** Let $E,F,G$ be edges with $E\cap F\cap G=\emptyset$ (a *good triple*). Put

$$
X=E\cap F,\quad Y=E\cap G,\quad Z=F\cap G,\quad P_E=E\setminus(F\cup G),\quad P_F=F\setminus(E\cup G),\quad P_G=G\setminus(E\cup F).
$$

A $2$-set meets $E$, $F$ and $G$ if and only if it has one point in each of the two sets of one of the six *candidate products*

$$
X\times Y,\quad X\times Z,\quad Y\times Z,\quad X\times P_G,\quad Y\times P_F,\quad Z\times P_E .
$$

If the family is $r$-uniform and $x,y,z$ denote $|X|,|Y|,|Z|$, then $|P_E|=r-x-y$, $|P_F|=r-x-z$, $|P_G|=r-y-z$.

*Proof.* Points outside $E\cup F\cup G$ have $\sigma=\emptyset$ and would need a partner in all three edges. Every other point has as $\sigma$ a nonempty proper subset of $\{E,F,G\}$; two such sets have union $\{E,F,G\}$ exactly when they are two distinct $2$-sets, or a $2$-set and the complementary singleton. The six cells $X,Y,Z,P_E,P_F,P_G$ are disjoint, which gives the sizes.
 ∎

**Remark 2.4 (relabelling).** Permuting $E,F,G$ permutes the three cells $X,Y,Z$, and every permutation of the cells arises; each private part stays attached to the cell it is paired with ($X$ with $P_G$, $Y$ with $P_F$, $Z$ with $P_E$). Consequently every lemma of Section 3, stated for cells named $X,Y,Z$ with sizes $x,y,z$, applies to a good triple with the three cells assigned to the roles $X,Y,Z$ in any order. We write, for instance, "Lemma 3.4 with $(x,y,z):=(z,y,m)$" for the application in which the cell of size $z$ plays the role $X$, the cell of size $y$ the role $Y$ and the cell of size $m$ the role $Z$.

**Lemma 2.5 (four edges).** Let $E,F,G,H$ be edges with $E\cap F\cap G=\emptyset$, and put $X=E\cap F$, $Y=E\cap G$, $Z=F\cap G$, $A=F\cap H$, $B=G\cap H$, $C=E\cap H$.
1. If $H$ is disjoint from $X\cup Y\cup Z$, then a $2$-set meets all four edges if and only if it lies in one of $X\times B$, $Y\times A$, $Z\times C$.
2. If $H$ is disjoint from $X\cup Y$, put $Q=Z\cap H$, $A'=A\setminus Q$, $B'=B\setminus Q$. Then a $2$-set meets all four edges if and only if it lies in one of $Q\times E$, $X\times B'$, $Y\times A'$, $(Z\setminus Q)\times C$.

*Proof.* (1) All triple intersections of the four edges are empty, so every $\sigma$ has size at most two, and two such sets cover the four edges only if they are complementary $2$-sets: $\{E,F\},\{G,H\}$, or $\{E,G\},\{F,H\}$, or $\{F,G\},\{E,H\}$. The corresponding cells are $X$ and $B$, $Y$ and $A$, $Z$ and $C$.
(2) Now the only triple intersection is $Q=F\cap G\cap H$, of type $\{F,G,H\}$; its points pair with exactly the points whose type contains $E$, i.e. the points of $E$. Points of type $\{G,H\}$, $\{F,H\}$, $\{F,G\}$, $\{E,H\}$ form $B'$, $A'$, $Z\setminus Q$ and $C$ respectively, and the complementary $2$-type pairs are as in (1). Singleton types need a partner of type of size three, i.e. in $Q$, whose partner must contain $E$; this is the product $Q\times E$ again.
 ∎

**Lemma 2.6 (balanced request).** Let $\mathcal H$ be $r$-uniform, let $E\ne G$ be edges with $|E\cap G|=q$, and let $T_0$ be an integer with $q\le T_0\le r$ and $\tau(\mathcal H)>T_0$, $T_0+q\ge2$. There is an edge $F\notin\{E,G\}$ with $E\cap F\cap G=\emptyset$ and

$$
|E\cap F|,\ |G\cap F|\ \le\ r-\lfloor (T_0+q)/2\rfloor \ \le\ r-\frac{T_0+q-1}{2}.
$$

*Proof.* Choose $E'\subseteq E$ and $G'\subseteq G$ containing $E\cap G$ with $|E'|=\lfloor (T_0+q)/2\rfloor $ and $|G'|=\lceil (T_0+q)/2\rceil $; this is possible because $q\le T_0$ and $T_0+q\le 2r-1$ (as $q\le r-1$ for distinct edges). Then $E'\cap G'=E\cap G$ and $|E'\cup G'|=T_0$. Request $F$ avoiding $E'\cup G'$ (Lemma 2.1). Then $|E\cap F|\le r-|E'|$, $|G\cap F|\le r-|G'|$, $F$ misses $E\cap G$, and $F\ne E,G$ because $E',G'$ are nonempty.
 ∎

**Lemma 2.7 (padding).** Let $\mathcal H$ have rank at most $k$ and property $(7,2)$. Adding to each edge $E$ a set of $k-|E|$ new vertices private to $E$ gives a $k$-uniform family $\mathcal H'$ with property $(7,2)$ and $\tau(\mathcal H')=\tau(\mathcal H)$.

*Proof.* Each padded edge contains the original, so transversals of subfamilies of $\mathcal H$ are transversals of the corresponding subfamilies of $\mathcal H'$; this gives property $(7,2)$ and $\tau(\mathcal H')\le\tau(\mathcal H)$. Conversely, in a transversal of $\mathcal H'$ replace each private vertex of an edge $E$ by any point of $E$ (edges are nonempty); the result is a transversal of $\mathcal H$ of no larger size.
 ∎

**Proposition 2.8 (the lower bound).** For every $k\ge2$, the complete $k$-uniform hypergraph on $N=\lceil 7k/4\rceil -1$ points has property $(7,2)$ and transversal number $\lceil 3k/4\rceil $. Hence $f(k,7)\ge\lceil 3k/4\rceil $.

*Proof.* Seven $k$-sets $A_1,\dots,A_7$ of $[N]$ (repetitions allowed; this also covers subfamilies of fewer than seven edges) have a transversal $\{v,w\}$ ($v=w$ allowed) if and only if no $A_i$ misses both $v$ and $w$. Hence they have no transversal of size at most two if and only if their complements $P_i=[N]\setminus A_i$ cover every point and every pair of $[N]$. Suppose they do. If every point lies in at least three $P_i$ then $\sum|P_i|\ge3N$; otherwise some point $a$ lies in at most two blocks, say only in $P_i$ and $P_j$ ($i=j$ allowed), every other point shares a block with $a$ and hence lies in $P_i\cup P_j$, so $|P_i|+|P_j|\ge N$. Either way some $|P_i|\ge3N/7$. But $|P_i|=N-k<3N/7$ because $N<7k/4$. Finally, a set is a transversal of the complete hypergraph iff its complement has fewer than $k$ points, so $\tau=N-k+1=\lceil 7k/4\rceil -k=\lceil 3k/4\rceil $.
 ∎

## 3. Closing lemmas for a good triple

**Standing assumptions for this section.** $\mathcal H$ is $r$-uniform, $T$ is an integer, $E,F,G$ is a good triple with the notation of Lemma 2.3, $x=|X|$, $y=|Y|$, $z=|Z|$ and $S=x+y+z$. Each lemma concludes that $\mathcal H$ contains a bad subfamily consisting of $E,F,G$ and at most four responses. By Lemma 2.2 it suffices, at each final stage, to exhibit requests (sets of at most $T$ points, where $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$) that together contain every $2$-set meeting all edges constructed so far. All subset sizes below are integers whenever the data are integers.

**Lemma 3.1 (small triple).** Suppose $x,y,z\le m\le r/2$ and

$$
\tau(\mathcal H)>B:=\Bigl\lceil\max\Bigl\{\frac{3r+m}{4},\ \frac{2r+2m}{3}\Bigr\}\Bigr\rceil .
$$

Then $\mathcal H$ contains a bad subfamily.

*Proof.* The construction is a parametrised form of Case 2 in the proof of [FKW, Lemma 1]. Since the hypothesis is symmetric, by Remark 2.4 we may assume $x\ge y\ge z$. Note $B\le r$ (both terms are at most $r$ as $m\le r/2$) and $B\ge 2m$ (since $(2r+2m)/3\ge2m$). Choose
- $A_F\subseteq P_F$ with $|A_F|=B-x-y$; this is possible since $0\le B-2m\le B-x-y\le r-x-z=|P_F|$, the last because $B\le r$ and $y\ge z$;
- $B_0\subseteq P_G$ with $|B_0|=\min(B-x,\ r-y-z)$, and put $C:=G\setminus(Y\cup B_0)=Z\cup(P_G\setminus B_0)$, so $c:=|C|=\max(r-B+x-y,\ z)$;
- $A_E\subseteq P_E$ with $|A_E|=\min(B-x-c,\ r-x-y)$; here $B-x-c\ge0$ because $B-x-z\ge B-2m\ge0$ and $B-x-(r-B+x-y)\ge 2B-r-2m\ge0$ (as $2B\ge(4r+4m)/3\ge r+2m$).

Request edges avoiding

$$
D_1=X\cup Y\cup A_F,\quad D_2=X\cup B_0,\quad D_3=X\cup C\cup A_E,\quad D_4=Y\cup Z\cup(P_E\setminus A_E)\cup(P_F\setminus A_F).
$$

*Sizes.* $|D_1|=B$, $|D_2|\le x+(B-x)=B$, $|D_3|\le x+c+(B-x-c)=B$. For $D_4$,

$$
|D_4|=y+z+\bigl(r-x-y-|A_E|\bigr)+\bigl(r-x-z-(B-x-y)\bigr)=r+2y-B+\max(0,\ r-y-B+c),
$$

and substituting $c$ gives $|D_4|=\max\{r-B+2y,\ 3(r-B)+x,\ 2(r-B)+y+z\}$. Each term is at most $B$: $2B\ge r+2m\ge r+2y$ (as $2B\ge(4r+4m)/3\ge r+2m$), $4B\ge3r+m\ge3r+x$, and $3B\ge2r+2m\ge2r+y+z$. All four requests have at most $B<\tau(\mathcal H)$ points.

*Coverage* (Lemma 2.3). $X\times Y\subseteq D_1$. $X\times Z\subseteq D_3$ since $Z\subseteq C$. $X\times P_G$: $P_G=B_0\cup(P_G\setminus B_0)$ with $B_0\subseteq D_2$ and $P_G\setminus B_0\subseteq C\subseteq D_3$. $Y\times Z\subseteq D_4$. $Y\times P_F$: points of $A_F$ are with $Y$ in $D_1$, the rest in $D_4$. $Z\times P_E$: points of $A_E$ are with $Z$ in $D_3$, the rest in $D_4$. Lemma 2.2 finishes the proof.
 ∎

**Lemma 3.2 (three response cases).** Suppose

$$
T\ge\max\Bigl\{S,\ r-x+z,\ r-y+z,\ r-x+\frac y2,\ r-y+\frac x2,\ \frac{r+2x+2y+z}{3}\Bigr\}
$$

and $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$. Then $\mathcal H$ contains a bad subfamily.

*Proof.* Request $H$ avoiding $X\cup Y\cup Z$ ($S\le T$ points). With $A=F\cap H$, $B=G\cap H$, $C=E\cap H$ (sizes $a,b,c$) we have $A\subseteq P_F$, $B\subseteq P_G$, $C\subseteq P_E$, hence

$$
a\le r-x-z,\qquad b\le r-y-z,\qquad c\le r-x-y,\qquad a+b+c\le r,
$$

and by Lemma 2.5(1) it remains to cover $X\times B$, $Y\times A$, $Z\times C$ with three requests of at most $T$ points. Note $T-x,T-y\ge0$ since $T\ge S$.

*Case $b\le T-x$.* Use $X\cup B$, $Y\cup Z\cup C\cup A_1$, $Y\cup A_2$, where $A=A_1\sqcup A_2$ with $|A_1|\le T-y-z-c$ and $|A_2|\le T-y$. Such a split exists because $T-y-z-c\ge T-y-z-(r-x-y)=T-(r-x+z)\ge0$ and $(T-y-z-c)+(T-y)\ge a$, i.e. $a+z+c\le 2T-2y$, which holds since $a+z+c\le(r-x-z)+z+(r-x-y)=2r-2x-y\le 2T-2y$ by $T\ge r-x+y/2$.

*Case $a\le T-y$.* Symmetric: use $Y\cup A$, $X\cup Z\cup C\cup B_1$, $X\cup B_2$, using $T\ge r-y+z$ and $T\ge r-y+x/2$.

*Case $b>T-x$ and $a>T-y$.* Choose $B_2\subseteq B$ with $|B_2|=T-x$ and $A_3\subseteq A$ with $|A_3|=T-y$, and use

$$
X\cup B_2,\qquad Y\cup A_3,\qquad X\cup Y\cup Z\cup C\cup(A\setminus A_3)\cup(B\setminus B_2).
$$

The first two have exactly $T$ points; the third has $S+c+a-(T-y)+b-(T-x)=a+b+c+2x+2y+z-2T\le r+2x+2y+z-2T\le T$ points. In each case every candidate product lies in one request.
 ∎

**Lemma 3.3 (padding one private part).** Suppose $T\le r$, $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$ and

$$
T\ge\max\Bigl\{S,\ \frac r2+y,\ \frac{r+2x-y+z}{2},\ \frac{r+2x+y+3z}{3}\Bigr\}.
$$

Then $\mathcal H$ contains a bad subfamily.

*Proof.* Request $H$ avoiding $X\cup Y\cup Z$ together with $T-S$ points of $P_F$; this fits because $0\le T-S\le r-x-z$, the latter being $T\le r+y$. With $A,B,C$ as in Lemma 3.2, now $a\le r-x-z-(T-S)=r-T+y$, $b\le r-y-z$, $a+b+c\le r$, and it remains to cover $X\times B$, $Y\times A$, $Z\times C$. Note $2(T-x-z)\ge r-y-z\ge b\ge0$ by the third term.

*Case $a\le T-y-z$.* Split $B=B_1\sqcup B_2$ with $|B_i|\le T-x-z$ and start the requests as $X\cup Z\cup B_1$, $X\cup Z\cup B_2$, $Y\cup Z\cup A$, all of size at most $T$. Their total size plus $c$ is at most $2x+y+3z+a+b+c\le r+2x+y+3z\le 3T$, so $C$ (which is disjoint from all three) can be distributed into the residual capacities. Every request contains $Z$, so $Z\times C$ is covered; the first two cover $X\times B$ and the third covers $Y\times A$.

*Case $a>T-y-z$.* Then $b+c\le r-a<r-T+y+z\le 2(T-x-z)$, the last inequality being the fourth term. Split $B\cup C$ into two parts of size at most $T-x-z$ and use $X\cup Z\cup(\text{part}_1)$, $X\cup Z\cup(\text{part}_2)$ and $Y\cup A$; the last has at most $y+r-T+y\le T$ points by the second term. Again every candidate product is covered.
 ∎

**Lemma 3.4 (a surviving triple cell).** Suppose $T\le r$, $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$ and

$$
T\ge\max\Bigl\{x+y,\ \frac r2+x,\ \frac r2+y,\ r+x-y-z,\ r-x+y-z,\ r-\frac S3,\ \frac{3r+S}{5},\ \frac{r+x+y+2z}{3},\ \frac{2r+3z}{4}\Bigr\}.
$$

Then $\mathcal H$ contains a bad subfamily.

*Proof.* Request $H$ avoiding $X\cup Y\cup Z_0$, where $Z_0\subseteq Z$ has size $\min(z,T-x-y)$. Put $Q=Z\cap H$, $A=(F\cap H)\setminus Q$, $B=(G\cap H)\setminus Q$, $C=E\cap H$, $V=Z\setminus Q$, $D=E\setminus(X\cup Y\cup C)$, with sizes $q,a,b,c,v=z-q,d=r-x-y-c$. Then $A\subseteq P_F$, $B\subseteq P_G$, $C\subseteq P_E$ and

$$
q\le(S-T)_+,\quad a\le r-x-z,\quad b\le r-y-z,\quad c\le r-x-y,\quad q+a+b+c\le r .
$$

By Lemma 2.5(2) we must cover $Q\times E$, $X\times B$, $Y\times A$, $V\times C$. We shall use three requests that all contain $Q$ and whose union contains $E$; then $Q\times E$ is covered.

*Two uniform bounds.* $q+x+b\le\max(r+x-y-z,\ r+2x-T)\le T$. Indeed if $S\le T$ then $q=0$ and $b\le r-y-z$; if $S>T$ then $|G\cap(X\cup Y\cup Z_0)|=y+(T-x-y)=T-x$, so $q+b=|G\cap H|\le r-T+x$. Symmetrically $q+y+a\le\max(r-x+y-z,\ r+2y-T)\le T$ (using $|F\cap(X\cup Y\cup Z_0)|=T-y$). Also $z\le T$, since $4T\ge2r+3z\ge5z$.

*Case 0: $c\le T-z$.* Start with $Q\cup X\cup B$, $Q\cup Y\cup A$, $Z\cup C$, each of size at most $T$. Their total plus $d$ equals $r+2q+a+b+z$. Using $a+b\le 2r-x-y-2z$: if $S\le T$ this is at most $3r-S\le3T$ (term $r-S/3$); if $S>T$ it is at most $3r-S+2(S-T)=3r+S-2T\le3T$ (term $(3r+S)/5$). Distribute $D$ (disjoint from all three) into the residual capacities.

In the remaining cases $c>T-z$; put $a_0=r+x+z-2T$ and $b_0=r+y+z-2T$.

*Case 1: $a<a_0$.* Start with $Q\cup X\cup B$, $Y\cup A\cup Z\cup C_2$, $Z\cup C_3$, where $C=C_2\sqcup C_3$, $|C_2|\le T-y-a-z$, $|C_3|\le T-z$. This is possible: $y+a+z< r+x+y+2z-2T\le T$ (term $(r+x+y+2z)/3$), and $a+c< a_0+(r-x-y)=2r+z-y-2T\le 2T-2z-y$ (term $(2r+3z)/4$), i.e. the two capacities sum to more than $c$. The total plus $d$ is $r+q+a+b+2z\le 2r+2z-c<2r+3z-T\le3T$. Distribute $D$.

*Case 2: $b<b_0$.* Symmetric to Case 1, exchanging $(X,B,x,b)$ with $(Y,A,y,a)$.

*Case 3: $a\ge a_0$ and $b\ge b_0$.* Put $u=c+z-T$; then $0<u\le c$ since $z\le T$. Choose $C_{12}\subseteq C$ with $|C_{12}|=u$, put $C_3=C\setminus C_{12}$ (so $|C_3|=T-z$), and choose an integer $t$ with

$$
\max(0,\ y+a+z+u-T)\ \le\ t\ \le\ \min(v,\ T-q-x-b-u).
$$

The interval is nonempty: $T-q-x-b-u=2T-x-z-(q+b+c)\ge0$ because $q+b+c\le r-a\le r-a_0$; $y+a+z+u-T\le v$ is $q+a+c\le 2T-y-z$, true because $q+a+c\le r-b\le r-b_0$; and $y+a+z+u-T\le T-q-x-b-u$ is $q+a+b+2c+x+y+3z\le4T$, which follows from $q+a+b+c\le r$, $c\le r-x-y$ and $2r+3z\le4T$. Split $V=V_{13}\sqcup V_{23}$ with $|V_{13}|=t$ and start with

$$
Q\cup X\cup B\cup C_{12}\cup V_{13},\qquad Q\cup Y\cup A\cup C_{12}\cup V_{23},\qquad Z\cup C_3 .
$$

The choice of $t$ makes the first two of size at most $T$ (using $q+v=z$), the third has exactly $T$ points, and the total plus $d$ is $r+q+a+b+c+3z-T\le 2r+3z-T\le 3T$. Distribute $D$.

In every case $X\times B$ and $Y\times A$ are covered by the first two requests, and $V\times C$ is covered since each part of $C$ lies in a request together with all of $V$ (in Case 3, $C_{12}$ lies in both of the first two requests, which together contain $V$, and $C_3$ lies with $Z\supseteq V$ in the third). All three requests contain $Q$ and their union contains $X\cup Y\cup C\cup D=E$.
 ∎

**Lemma 3.5 (static template S1).** Suppose $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$ and there are integers $x_1,y_1,z_1$ with $0\le x_1\le x$, $0\le y_1\le y$, $0\le z_1\le z$ and

$$
x_1+y_1+z_1\le T,\qquad y_1+z_1\ge r+x-T,\qquad x_1+z_1\ge r+y-T,\qquad x_1+y_1\ge r+z-T.
$$

Then $\mathcal H$ contains a bad subfamily.

*Proof.* Split $X=X_1\sqcup X_2$, $Y=Y_1\sqcup Y_2$, $Z=Z_1\sqcup Z_2$ with $|X_1|=x_1$, $|Y_1|=y_1$, $|Z_1|=z_1$, and request (all four at once)

$$
R_0=X_1\cup Y_1\cup Z_1,\quad R_X=X\cup P_G\cup Y_2\cup Z_2,\quad R_Y=Y\cup P_F\cup X_2\cup Z_2,\quad R_Z=Z\cup P_E\cup X_2\cup Y_2 .
$$

Their sizes are $x_1+y_1+z_1$, $r+x-y_1-z_1$, $r+y-x_1-z_1$, $r+z-x_1-y_1$, all at most $T$. Coverage: $X\times P_G\subseteq R_X$, $Y\times P_F\subseteq R_Y$, $Z\times P_E\subseteq R_Z$. For $(p,q)\in X\times Y$: if $q\in Y_2$ then $\{p,q\}\subseteq R_X$; if $p\in X_2$ then $\{p,q\}\subseteq R_Y$; otherwise $(p,q)\in X_1\times Y_1\subseteq R_0$. The products $X\times Z$ (via $R_X$, $R_Z$, $R_0$) and $Y\times Z$ (via $R_Y$, $R_Z$, $R_0$) are handled identically.
 ∎

**Lemma 3.6 (static template S2).** Suppose $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$, and put $P=\max(0,r+y-x-z-T)$ and $Q=\max(0,r+x-y-z-T)$. If $x\le T$, $y\le T$ and

$$
\text{(i) } T\ge r-x+z+P+Q,\qquad \text{(ii) } T\ge y+z+Q,\qquad \text{(iii) } 2T\ge r+y+2z+P+2Q,
$$

then $\mathcal H$ contains a bad subfamily.

*Proof.* Since $y\le T$ we have $P\le r-x-z=|P_F|$, and since $x\le T$ we have $Q\le r-y-z=|P_G|$. Split $P_F=V_1\sqcup V_2$ with $|V_1|=P$ and $P_G=W_0\sqcup W_{13}$ with $|W_{13}|=Q$. Put $U_1=T-r+x-z-P-Q$ and $L=x+y+z+Q-T$. The integer interval $[\max(0,L),\min(x,U_1)]$ is nonempty: $0\le U_1$ is (i), $L\le x$ is (ii), $L\le U_1$ is (iii), and $0\le x$. Choose $x_{01}$ in it and split $X=X_{01}\sqcup X_{03}$ with $|X_{01}|=x_{01}$. Request

$$
R_0=X\cup W_0,\quad R_1=X_{01}\cup Y\cup Z\cup P_E\cup V_1\cup W_{13},\quad R_2=Y\cup V_2,\quad R_3=X_{03}\cup Y\cup Z\cup W_{13}.
$$

Sizes: $|R_0|=x+r-y-z-Q\le T$ by the definition of $Q$; $|R_2|=y+r-x-z-P\le T$ by the definition of $P$; $|R_1|=x_{01}+r-x+z+P+Q\le T$ as $x_{01}\le U_1$; $|R_3|=x-x_{01}+y+z+Q\le T$ as $x_{01}\ge L$. Coverage: $X\times P_G$: $X\times W_0\subseteq R_0$, $X_{01}\times W_{13}\subseteq R_1$, $X_{03}\times W_{13}\subseteq R_3$. $Y\times P_F$: $Y\times V_1\subseteq R_1$, $Y\times V_2\subseteq R_2$. $Z\times P_E\subseteq R_1$. $X\times Y$ and $X\times Z$: $X_{01}$ with $Y\cup Z$ in $R_1$, $X_{03}$ with $Y\cup Z$ in $R_3$. $Y\times Z\subseteq R_1$.
 ∎

**Lemma 3.7 (scaling and monotonicity).** Each hypothesis of Lemmas 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 and 3.6, other than $T\le r$, has the form $g(r,x,y,z,T)\ge0$ with $g$ positively homogeneous of degree one and nondecreasing in $T$. Consequently, if these hypotheses hold for the real numbers $(1,x/r,y/r,z/r,\beta)$, then they hold for $(r,x,y,z,T)$ for every real $T\ge\beta r$.

*Proof.* For Lemmas 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 each hypothesis is $T-\ell(r,x,y,z)\ge0$ or $cT-\ell\ge0$ with $c>0$ and $\ell$ linear. For Lemma 3.6, $P$ and $Q$ are of the form $\max(0,\ell-T)$, which is positively homogeneous and nonincreasing in $T$; each of $T-x$, $T-y$, $T-(r-x+z)-P-Q$, $T-y-z-Q$, $2T-(r+y+2z)-P-2Q$ is then homogeneous and nondecreasing in $T$. Homogeneity transfers the inequalities from $(1,x/r,y/r,z/r,\beta)$ to $(r,x,y,z,\beta r)$, and monotonicity to every $T\ge\beta r$.
 ∎

## 4. The local closing proposition

Throughout this section and the next, $\beta=173/200$ and $e:=1-\beta=27/200$.

**Proposition 4.1 (local closing lemma).** Let $r$ and $T$ be integers with $\beta r+3\le T\le r$, and let $\mathcal H$ be an $r$-uniform family with $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$. Let $E,F,G$ be a good triple whose three pair intersections have sizes $m\ge y\ge z$, where

$$
m\le\frac{23r}{50}\qquad\text{and}\qquad m+2y\le\frac{227r}{200}=(2-\beta)r .
$$

Then $\mathcal H$ contains a bad subfamily. No hypothesis on other pair intersections of $\mathcal H$ is needed.

*Proof.* Write $\bar m=m/r$, $\bar y=y/r$, $\bar z=z/r$. The case distinctions below refer to these normalised values; to lighten notation we drop the bars, so in each case $m,y,z$ are real numbers with

$$
0\le z\le y\le m\le\tfrac{92}{200},\qquad m+2y\le\tfrac{227}{200}. \tag{R}
$$

In cases (b) and (c) we verify the hypotheses of the lemma used at $r=1$, $T=\beta$; by Lemma 3.7 they then hold for the actual integers $r$ and $T\ge\beta r$ (and $T\le r$ is given). Case (a) and the rounding in case (c4) are treated directly at the integer level.

**(a) $m\le119/400$.** Here we return to the unnormalised size $m\le\tfrac{119}{400}r$. Apply Lemma 3.1 with this $m$ (all three intersections are at most $m\le r/2$). Its budget satisfies $(2r+2m)/3\le(2+2\cdot\tfrac{119}{400})r/3=\beta r$ and $(3r+m)/4\le(3+\tfrac{119}{400})r/4=\tfrac{1319}{1600}r<\beta r$, so $B\le\lceil \beta r\rceil \le T<\tau(\mathcal H)$. (This case uses its own budget $B$, not $T$.)

**(b) $m>119/400$ and $y\le73/200$.**

*(b2) $y-z>m-e$.* Lemma 3.3 with $(x,y,z):=(m,y,z)$. Its conditions are: $S\le\beta$: from $z<y-m+e$ we get $S<2y+e\le\tfrac{146+27}{200}=\beta$. $\tfrac12+y\le\beta$: $y\le\tfrac{73}{200}$. $\tfrac{1+2m-y+z}{2}\le\beta$, i.e. $2m-y+z\le\tfrac{146}{200}$: $2m-y+z<m+e\le\tfrac{92+27}{200}$. $\tfrac{1+2m+y+3z}{3}\le\beta$, i.e. $2m+y+3z\le\tfrac{319}{200}$: $2m+y+3z<4y-m+3e\le3y+\tfrac{81}{200}\le\tfrac{219+81}{200}$.

*(b3) $y-z\le m-e$ and $S<81/200$.* Lemma 3.3 with $(x,y,z):=(z,y,m)$. Conditions: $S<\tfrac{81}{200}\le\beta$; $\tfrac12+y\le\beta$; $2z-y+m\le z+m\le S<\tfrac{146}{200}$; $2z+y+3m\le3S<\tfrac{243}{200}\le\tfrac{319}{200}$.

*(b1) $y-z\le m-e$ and $S\ge81/200$.* Lemma 3.4 with $(x,y,z):=(z,y,m)$, so its nine conditions read (with $S=m+y+z$):
1. $z+y\le\beta$: $z+y\le2y\le\tfrac{146}{200}$.
2. $\tfrac12+z\le\beta$ and (3) $\tfrac12+y\le\beta$: from $z\le y\le\tfrac{73}{200}$.
4. $1+z-y-m\le\beta$, i.e. $y+m-z\ge e$: $y+m-z\ge m>\tfrac{119}{400}>e$.
5. $1-z+y-m\le\beta$, i.e. $y-z\le m-e$: the case hypothesis.
6. $1-S/3\le\beta$, i.e. $S\ge3e=\tfrac{81}{200}$: the case hypothesis.
7. $\tfrac{3+S}{5}\le\beta$, i.e. $S\le5\beta-3=\tfrac{265}{200}$: $S\le m+2y\le\tfrac{227}{200}$.
8. $\tfrac{1+z+y+2m}{3}\le\beta$, i.e. $z+y+2m\le\tfrac{319}{200}$: $z+y\le2y\le\tfrac{227}{200}-m$, so $z+y+2m\le\tfrac{227}{200}+m\le\tfrac{227+92}{200}$. (This is where $m\le23/50$ is used; it is tight at $m=23/50$, $z=y$, $m+2y=227/200$.)
9. $\tfrac{2+3m}{4}\le\beta$, i.e. $m\le\tfrac{292}{600}$: $m\le\tfrac{92}{200}$.

Cases (b1), (b2), (b3) exhaust (b).

**(c) $y>73/200$** (then $m\ge y>119/400$). Put $u=m+y$ and $d=m-y\ge0$. From (R) and $m\ge y>\tfrac{73}{200}$:

$$
\begin{gathered}
m\le\tfrac{227}{200}-2y<\tfrac{81}{200},\qquad \tfrac{146}{200}<u<\tfrac{154}{200},\qquad d<\tfrac{8}{200},\\
2m-y\le\tfrac{454}{200}-5y<\tfrac{89}{200},\qquad 2m+3y\le\tfrac{454}{200}-y<\tfrac{381}{200},\qquad 2m+y\le\tfrac{454}{200}-3y<\tfrac{235}{200}.
\end{gathered} \tag{C}
$$

(For the last three use $m\le\tfrac{227}{200}-2y$ and $y>\tfrac{73}{200}$.)

*(c1) $z\le\tfrac{319}{200}-2u$.* Lemma 3.2 with $(x,y,z):=(m,y,z)$. Conditions: $\tfrac{1+2u+z}{3}\le\beta$ is the case hypothesis. $S=u+z\le\tfrac{319}{200}-u<\tfrac{173}{200}$. $1-y+z\le\beta$, i.e. $z\le y-e$: from $z\le\tfrac{319}{200}-2m-2y$ it suffices that $2m+3y\ge\tfrac{346}{200}$, and indeed $2m+3y>5\cdot\tfrac{73}{200}$; then also $1-m+z\le1-y+z\le\beta$. $1-m+y/2\le\beta$, i.e. $m-y/2\ge e$: $m-y/2\ge y/2>\tfrac{36.5}{200}$. $1-y+m/2\le\beta$, i.e. $y-m/2\ge e$: $y-m/2>\tfrac{73-40.5}{200}=\tfrac{32.5}{200}$.

*(c2) $z>\tfrac{319}{200}-2u$ and $z<e-d$.* Lemma 3.6 with $(x,y,z):=(y,m,z)$ (the $y$-cell plays the role $X$, the $m$-cell the role $Y$). At $r=1$, $T=\beta$: $P=\max(0,e+d-z)=e+d-z>0$ (since $z<e-d\le e+d$) and $Q=\max(0,e-d-z)=e-d-z>0$. The conditions $X=y\le\beta$ and $Y=m\le\beta$ hold by (C). Then
- (i) $\beta\ge1-y+z+P+Q=1-y-z+2e$, i.e. $z\ge\tfrac{81}{200}-y$;
- (ii) $\beta\ge m+z+Q=m-d+e=y+e$, i.e. $y\le\tfrac{146}{200}$, which holds by (C);
- (iii) $2\beta\ge1+m+2z+P+2Q=1+m-d-z+3e=1+y-z+3e$, i.e. $z\ge y-\tfrac{65}{200}$.

Both lower bounds follow from $z>\tfrac{319}{200}-2u$: indeed $\tfrac{319}{200}-2u\ge\tfrac{81}{200}-y$ is $2m+y\le\tfrac{238}{200}$, and $\tfrac{319}{200}-2u\ge y-\tfrac{65}{200}$ is $2m+3y\le\tfrac{384}{200}$; both hold by (C).

*(c3) $z>\tfrac{319}{200}-2u$, $z\ge e-d$ and $z\le\tfrac12(\tfrac{146}{200}-y)$.* Lemma 3.6 with $(x,y,z):=(m,y,z)$. Now $P=\max(0,e-d-z)=0$ and $Q=\max(0,e+d-z)$; $m,y\le\beta$ by (C). The conditions become (i) $1-m+z+Q\le\beta$, (ii) $y+z+Q\le\beta$, (iii) $1+y+2z+2Q\le2\beta$.
- If $Q=0$ ($z\ge e+d$): (i) is $z\le m-e$, which follows from $z\le\tfrac{73}{200}-\tfrac y2$ and $2m+y\ge\tfrac{219}{200}>1$ (so $\tfrac{73}{200}-\tfrac y2\le m-e$); (ii) $y+z\le\tfrac{73}{200}+\tfrac y2<\tfrac{73+40.5}{200}<\beta$; (iii) is $y+2z\le\tfrac{146}{200}$, the case hypothesis.
- If $Q>0$ ($z<e+d$): (i) becomes $1+e-y\le\beta$, i.e. $y\ge2e=\tfrac{54}{200}$; (ii) becomes $m+e\le\beta$, i.e. $m\le\tfrac{146}{200}$; (iii) becomes $1+y+2d+2e\le2\beta$, i.e. $2m-y\le\tfrac{92}{200}$, true by (C).

*(c4) $z>\tfrac12(\tfrac{146}{200}-y)$* (and $z>\tfrac{319}{200}-2u$, $z\ge e-d$). First,

$$
z\ \ge\ \max\Bigl(e+d,\ u-\tfrac{119}{200}\Bigr). \tag{$*$}
$$

Indeed $\tfrac12(\tfrac{146}{200}-y)\ge e+d$ is equivalent to $2m-y\le\tfrac{92}{200}$, and $\tfrac12(\tfrac{146}{200}-y)\ge u-\tfrac{119}{200}$ is equivalent to $2m+3y\le\tfrac{384}{200}$; both hold by (C). We apply Lemma 3.5 with $(x,y,z):=(m,y,z)$ and splits $(m_1,y_1,z_1)$ chosen as follows (normalised; the requirements at $r=1$, $T=\beta$ are $0\le m_1\le m$, $0\le y_1\le y$, $0\le z_1\le z$, $m_1+y_1+z_1\le\beta$, $y_1+z_1\ge e+m$, $m_1+z_1\ge e+y$, $m_1+y_1\ge e+z$).
- *Split A, if $3z\ge e+u$:* $m_1=\tfrac12(e+y+z-m)$, $y_1=\tfrac12(e+m+z-y)$, $z_1=\tfrac12(e+m+y-z)$. The three pair sums equal $e+m$, $e+y$, $e+z$ exactly; the total is $\tfrac12(3e+S)\le\beta$ because $S\le m+2y\le\tfrac{227}{200}\le2\beta-3e=\tfrac{265}{200}$. Bounds: $m_1\ge0$ as $z\ge e+d\ge d-e$; $m_1\le m$ iff $z\le3m-y-e$, true as $z\le y$ and $2y+e\le3m$ (since $3m-2y\ge y>e$); $y_1\ge0$ clearly; $y_1\le y$ iff $z\le3y-m-e$, true as $z\le y$ and $m+e\le2y$ (since $d<\tfrac{8}{200}<y-e$); $z_1\ge0$ as $z\le y\le m$; $z_1\le z$ iff $3z\ge e+u$.
- *Split B, if $3z<e+u$:* $z_1=z$, $y_1=e+m-z$, $m_1=e+y-z$. Pair sums: $y_1+z_1=e+m$, $m_1+z_1=e+y$, $m_1+y_1=2e+u-2z\ge e+z$ iff $3z\le e+u$. Total $2e+u-z\le\beta$ iff $z\ge u-\tfrac{119}{200}$, which is $(*)$. Bounds: $y_1\ge0$ as $z\le m$; $y_1\le y$ iff $z\ge e+d$, which is $(*)$; $m_1\ge0$ as $z\le y$; $m_1\le m$ iff $z\ge e-d$.

*Integer rounding.* At the integer level take $\hat m_1=\lceil m_1r\rceil $, $\hat y_1=\lceil y_1r\rceil $, $\hat z_1=\lceil z_1r\rceil $, where $m_1,y_1,z_1$ are computed from the normalised cell sizes. Since the cell sizes $m,y,z$ (unnormalised) are integers and $m_1r\le m$ etc., the rounded splits still satisfy $0\le\hat m_1\le m$ etc.; the three lower bounds on pair sums, e.g. $\hat y_1+\hat z_1\ge (e+\bar m)r=r+m-\beta r\ge r+m-T$, survive rounding up; and $\hat m_1+\hat y_1+\hat z_1<(m_1+y_1+z_1)r+3\le\beta r+3\le T$. Hence Lemma 3.5 applies with the integer budget $T$. This is the only place where the additive $3$ in $T\ge\beta r+3$ is used.

*Exhaustiveness.* The cases are defined by an if-then-else chain: (a); otherwise (b) if $y\le\tfrac{73}{200}$, split into (b2), then (b3), then (b1); otherwise (c), split into (c1), then (c2), then (c3), then (c4). Each later case is the complement of the earlier ones within (c), which is how the inequalities $z>\tfrac{319}{200}-2u$ and $z\ge e-d$ were used in (c2)–(c4). In every case a lemma of Section 3 produces a bad subfamily.
 ∎

**Remark 4.2.** The proof never uses property $(7,2)$ or any information about pair intersections other than those of $E,F,G$; it only uses $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$. The condition $m+2y\le(2-\beta)r$ is what a balanced request of size at least $\beta r+1$ guarantees (Lemma 2.6), while the bounds $y,z\le m$ on the other two intersections are supplied by the maximality of $m$ in Section 6. Neither intersectingness nor any bound on $\nu(\mathcal H)$ is assumed.

## 5. Two lemmas on intersection gaps

**Lemma 5.1 (extending a gap to $r/2$).** Let $h=23/50$, $\ell=43/200$, $r\ge1000$, and let $\mathcal H$ be an $r$-uniform family with $\tau(\mathcal H)>\lceil \beta r\rceil +10$ and no pair intersection in $[\ell r,hr]$. Then $\mathcal H$ contains a bad subfamily or has no pair intersection in $[hr,r/2]$.

*Proof.* Put $T=\lceil \beta r\rceil +4\le r$ and $h_0=\lfloor hr\rfloor $. Suppose $E,F$ are edges with $X=E\cap F$ and $x=|X|\in[hr,r/2]$. Lemma 2.6 with $T_0=\lceil \beta r\rceil $ gives an edge $G\ne E,F$ with $E\cap F\cap G=\emptyset$ and

$$
|E\cap G|,|F\cap G|\le r-\frac{\beta r+x-1}{2}\le\Bigl(1-\frac{\beta+h}{2}\Bigr)r+\frac12=\frac{67.5}{200}r+\frac12<hr .
$$

By the gap, $Y=E\cap G$ and $Z=F\cap G$ have sizes $y,z<\ell r$. Put $S=x+y+z$. Recall $|P_E|=r-x-y$, $|P_F|=r-x-z$, $|P_G|=r-y-z$.

*Case $S\le T$.* Let $p=(r-x-y-h_0)_+$, $t=(r-x-z-h_0)_+$, choose $P_1\subseteq P_E$, $P_2\subseteq P_F$ of sizes $p,t$, and let $D=X\cup Y\cup Z\cup P_1\cup P_2\cup W$, where $W\subseteq P_G$ is chosen so that $|D|=T$. Here $C:=|X\cup Y\cup Z\cup P_1\cup P_2|=x+\max(y,r-x-h_0)+\max(z,r-x-h_0)$, and the four possible values are $S\le T$, $r-h_0+y$ and $r-h_0+z$ (both $<(1-h+\ell)r+1=\tfrac{151}{200}r+1<T$), and $2r-x-2h_0\le(2-3h)r+2=0.62r+2<T$. So $C\le T$, and $|W|=T-C\le T-S\le r-y-z$ (as $T\le r+x$). Request $H$ avoiding $D$. Then $E\cap H\subseteq P_E\setminus P_1$ has at most $\min(r-x-y,h_0)\le hr$ points, and $H\ne E$ (as $H$ misses $X\ne\emptyset$); by the gap $|E\cap H|<\ell r$, and likewise $|F\cap H|<\ell r$. Further $b:=|G\cap H|\le r-y-z-|W|=r-T+x+p+t$. All triple intersections of $E,F,G,H$ are empty, so by Lemma 2.5(1) it suffices to cover $X\times B$, $Y\times(F\cap H)$, $Z\times(E\cap H)$, where $B=G\cap H$. Split $B=B_1\sqcup B_2$ with $|B_i|\le\lceil b/2\rceil $ and request $X\cup B_1$, $X\cup B_2$, $Y\cup Z\cup(E\cap H)\cup(F\cap H)$. The last has fewer than $4\ell r=0.86r<T$ points. For the first two, $x+\lceil b/2\rceil \le\tfrac12(r+3x+p+t-T+1)$, and expanding the positive parts, $r+3x+p+t$ is at most the maximum of

$$
r+3x,\quad 2r+2x-y-h_0,\quad 2r+2x-z-h_0,\quad 3r+x-y-z-2h_0,
$$

which for $x\le r/2$, $y,z\ge0$, $h_0>hr-1$ is at most $\max(2.5r,\ 2.54r+1,\ 2.58r+2)=2.58r+2$. Since $3T\ge3\beta r+12=2.595r+12$, we get $x+\lceil b/2\rceil \le T$. By Lemma 2.2, $E,F,G,H$ and the three responses form a bad subfamily.

*Case $S>T$.* Since $x+y<(\tfrac12+\ell)r=0.715r<T$, request $H$ avoiding $X\cup Y\cup Z_0$ with $Z_0\subseteq Z$, $|Z_0|=T-x-y\le z$. With $Q=Z\cap H$, $A=(F\cap H)\setminus Q$, $B=(G\cap H)\setminus Q$, $C=E\cap H$ (sizes $q,a,b,c$) we have $q\le S-T$, $b\le r-y-z$, and

$$
c\le r-x-y<r-T+z<(e+\ell)r-4<hr,\qquad q+a=|F\cap H|\le r-(T-y)<(e+\ell)r-4<hr ,
$$

using $x+y>T-z$, $|F\cap(X\cup Y\cup Z_0)|=T-y$, $y,z<\ell r$ and $e+\ell=0.35<h$. As $H\ne E,F$ (it misses $X$), the gap gives $c<\ell r$ and $q+a<\ell r$. By Lemma 2.5(2) we must cover $Q\times E$, $X\times B$, $Y\times A$ and $(Z\setminus Q)\times C$. Start with

$$
R_1=X\cup Q\cup B_1,\qquad R_2=X\cup Q\cup B_2,\qquad R_3=Y\cup Z\cup A\cup C,
$$

where $B=B_1\sqcup B_2$, $|B_i|\le\lceil b/2\rceil $. Using $q\le x+y+z-T$, $x\le r/2$ and $y+z<2\ell r$,

$$
|R_i|\le x+q+\frac{b+1}{2}\le 2x+\frac{y+z}{2}+\frac r2-T+\frac12<\Bigl(\frac32+\ell-\beta\Bigr)r-\frac72=0.85r-3.5<T\quad(i=1,2),
$$

and $|R_3|<4\ell r<T$. The set $D:=E\setminus(X\cup Y\cup C)$ is disjoint from $R_1,R_2,R_3$, and the total of the three sizes plus $|D|=r-x-y-c$ is

$$
r+x+z+2q+a+b\le 2r+x-y+q+(q+a)<2r+2x+z-T+\ell r\le(3+2\ell)r-T=3.43r-T\le3T,
$$

because $4T\ge3.46r+16$. Distribute $D$ into the residual capacities. Now every request contains $Q$ (as $Q\subseteq Z$) and their union contains $X\cup Y\cup C\cup D=E$, so $Q\times E$ is covered; $R_1,R_2$ cover $X\times B$ and $R_3$ covers $Y\times A$ and $(Z\setminus Q)\times C$. Lemma 2.2 gives a bad subfamily of seven edges.
 ∎

**Lemma 5.2 (two large pair cells).** Let $\mathcal H$ be $r$-uniform and suppose every pair intersection is at most $m$ or greater than $r/2$, where $m\le r/4$. Let $E,F,G,H$ be edges with all four triple intersections empty, $X=E\cap F$, $B=G\cap H$ with $x=|X|>r/2$, $b=|B|>r/2$, and suppose the other four pair cells $Y=E\cap G$, $Z=F\cap G$, $A=F\cap H$, $C=E\cap H$ each have at most $m$ points. If $T\le r$ is an integer with $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$ and

$$
T\ge\lceil r/2\rceil +2m,\qquad T\ge x+m,\qquad 3T\ge2x+b+\lceil r/2\rceil +2m,
$$

then $\mathcal H$ contains a bad subfamily.

*Proof.* Put $U=Y\cup Z\cup A\cup C$ (a disjoint union), $s=|Y|+|Z|\le2m$, $t=|A|+|C|\le2m$, and

$$
p=\lceil r/2\rceil -\min(s,t),\qquad q=T-\lceil r/2\rceil -\max(s,t).
$$

Then $p\ge0$ (as $2m\le r/2$), $q\ge0$ (first condition), $p\le\lceil r/2\rceil \le b$, and $q\le T-\lceil r/2\rceil \le\lfloor r/2\rfloor <x$. Choose $B_0\subseteq B$, $X_0\subseteq X$ of sizes $p,q$ and request $I$ avoiding $U\cup B_0\cup X_0$, a set of exactly $T$ points. Since $G\setminus(Y\cup Z\cup B_0)$ has $r-s-p=\lfloor r/2\rfloor +\min(s,t)-s\le\lfloor r/2\rfloor $ points, $|G\cap I|\le r/2$; likewise $|H\cap I|\le r-t-p\le\lfloor r/2\rfloor $. Hence $I\ne G,H$ and, by the gap, $|G\cap I|,|H\cap I|\le m$. In particular $d:=|B\cap I|\le m$, and $x_I:=|X\cap I|\le x-q$.

By Lemma 2.5(1) the $2$-sets meeting $E,F,G,H$ lie in $X\times B$, $Y\times A$ or $Z\times C$; the last two products lie in $U$ and are missed by $I$. Choose $B_1\subseteq B$ with $B\cap I\subseteq B_1$ and $|B_1|=\min(b,T-x)$ (possible since $T-x\ge m\ge d$), and request edges avoiding

$$
X\cup B_1\qquad\text{and}\qquad (X\cap I)\cup(B\setminus B_1).
$$

The first has at most $T$ points. The second has $x_I+\max(0,b-T+x)$ points; if $b\le T-x$ this is $x_I\le x\le T$, and otherwise it is at most $2x+b-q-T\le 2x+b-T+\lceil r/2\rceil +2m-T\le T$ by the third condition. Now let $(v,w)\in X\times B$. If $w\in B_1$, the first response misses both points. Otherwise $w\notin I$ (as $B\cap I\subseteq B_1$), so if $\{v,w\}$ meets $I$ then $v\in X\cap I$ and $\{v,w\}$ lies in the second request. So the seven edges $E,F,G,H,I$ and the two responses form a bad subfamily.
 ∎

**Lemma 5.3 (conditional finishing lemma).** Let $5/6\le\beta'<1$, let $r$ be an integer with $T:=\lceil \beta' r\rceil +4\le r$, and let $\mathcal H$ be an $r$-uniform family with property $(7,2)$ in which every pair intersection is at most $\tfrac{3\beta'-2}{2}r$ or greater than $r/2$. Then $\tau(\mathcal H)\le T$.

*Proof.* Suppose $\tau(\mathcal H)>T$. Requesting an edge avoiding $T$ points of some edge gives a pair intersection at most $r-T<r/2$, so the largest pair intersection $m$ not exceeding $r/2$ exists, and $m\le\tfrac{3\beta'-2}{2}r\le r/2$. Take $E,G$ with $|E\cap G|=m$ and apply Lemma 2.6 with $T_0=T$: we obtain $F$ with $E\cap F\cap G=\emptyset$ and $|E\cap F|,|G\cap F|\le r-\lfloor (T+m)/2\rfloor $.

*If both are at most $r/2$*, they are at most $m$ by maximality, and Lemma 3.1 applies to $E,F,G$: its budget is at most $\lceil \beta' r\rceil \le T$, because $\tfrac{2r+2m}{3}\le\beta' r$ is equivalent to $m\le\tfrac{3\beta'-2}{2}r$, and $\tfrac{3r+m}{4}\le\tfrac{4+3\beta'}{8}r\le\beta' r$ as $\beta'\ge4/5$. This contradicts property $(7,2)$.

*Otherwise* one of them exceeds $r/2$; exchanging the names $E,G$ we may assume $X:=E\cap F$ has $x>r/2$, and then $Z:=F\cap G$ has $z\le r-x<r/2$, so $z\le m$; put $Y:=E\cap G$ ($|Y|=m$). We have $x\le r-\lfloor (T+m)/2\rfloor \le r-\tfrac{T+m}{2}+\tfrac12$. Moreover $m\le r-T$: otherwise $T+m\ge r+1$, $\lfloor (T+m)/2\rfloor \ge\lceil r/2\rceil $, and $x\le\lfloor r/2\rfloor $, a contradiction. Hence $m\le r/6-4<r/4$ and

$$
x+2m\le r-\tfrac T2+\tfrac{3m}{2}+\tfrac12\le\tfrac{5r-4T+1}{2}<T .
$$

Request $H$ avoiding $X\cup Y\cup Z$ together with $T-x-m-z$ points of $P_G$; this number is positive (as $x+m+z\le x+2m<T$) and at most $r-m-z=|P_G|$ (as $T\le r+x$). In particular $H\ne G$, and $H\ne E,F$ as $H$ misses $X$. Then $E\cap H\subseteq P_E$ and $F\cap H\subseteq P_F$ have fewer than $r/2$ points and hence at most $m$ points, and $b:=|G\cap H|\le r-(T-x)$, since $H$ avoids $T-x$ points of $G$.

*If $b\le r/2$*, then $b\le m$, and $E,G,H$ is a good triple ($H$ misses $Y$) with all pair intersections at most $m$; Lemma 3.1 gives a contradiction as before.

*If $b>r/2$*, all triple intersections of $E,F,G,H$ are empty and Lemma 5.2 applies (its gap hypothesis holds by the definition of $m$, and $m\le r/4$). Its conditions hold: $\lceil r/2\rceil +2m\le\lceil r/2\rceil +2r-2T\le T$ since $3T\ge\tfrac52r+12$; $x+m\le r-\tfrac T2+\tfrac m2+\tfrac12\le\tfrac32r-T+\tfrac12\le T$; and, using $b\le r-T+x$ and $x\le r-\tfrac{T+m}{2}+\tfrac12$,

$$
2x+b+\lceil r/2\rceil +2m\le 3x+r-T+\tfrac r2+\tfrac12+2m\le\tfrac{9r+m-5T+4}{2}\le3T,
$$

the last because $m\le r-T$ and $12T\ge10r+4$. Lemma 5.2 contradicts property $(7,2)$.
 ∎

## 6. Proof of Theorem 1.1

Let $k\ge1000$, $r=k$, $\beta=173/200$, $h=23/50$, $\ell=43/200$ (so $\ell=2-\beta-2h$), and let $\mathcal H$ be an $r$-uniform family with property $(7,2)$. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $\tau(\mathcal H)>K:=\lceil \beta r\rceil +10$. Note $K\le r$ (as $\tfrac{27}{200}r\ge11$). By Lemma 2.7 this also covers families of rank at most $k$.

**Step 1: no pair intersection in $[\ell r,hr]$.** Let $h_0=\lfloor hr\rfloor $. Some pair intersection is at most $r-K<h_0$ (request an edge avoiding $K$ points of an edge). Let $m$ be the largest pair intersection that is at most $h_0$, attained by $E,G$. Suppose $m\ge\ell r$. Lemma 2.6 with $T_0=K$ gives $F\ne E,G$ with $E\cap F\cap G=\emptyset$ and

$$
|E\cap F|,|G\cap F|\le r-\frac{K+m-1}{2}\le r-\frac{\beta r+10+\ell r-1}{2}=hr-4.5<h_0,
$$

using $\beta+\ell=2-2h$. By the maximality of $m$ both are at most $m$. Exchange the names $E,G$ if necessary so that $y:=|E\cap F|\ge z:=|G\cap F|$. Then $m\le h_0\le hr=\tfrac{23}{50}r$ and

$$
m+2y\le m+2r-(K+m-1)=2r-K+1\le(2-\beta)r-9<\tfrac{227}{200}r .
$$

Proposition 4.1 with $T=K$ (note $\beta r+3\le K\le r$) produces a bad subfamily, contradicting property $(7,2)$. Hence $m<\ell r$. Consequently every pair intersection is either less than $\ell r$ or at least $h_0+1>hr$.

**Step 2: no pair intersection in $[hr,r/2]$.** This is Lemma 5.1 (the alternative "bad subfamily" is excluded by property $(7,2)$).

**Step 3.** Every pair intersection is now less than $\ell r$ or greater than $r/2$. Since $\ell=\tfrac{43}{200}\le\tfrac{3\beta-2}{2}=\tfrac{119}{400}$, $\beta\ge5/6$ and $\lceil \beta r\rceil +4\le r$, Lemma 5.3 (with $\beta'=\beta$) gives $\tau(\mathcal H)\le\lceil \beta r\rceil +4<K$, a contradiction. This proves Theorem 1.1. ∎

**Remark 6.1 (rounding).** The additive constant $10$ arises as follows: Step 1 needs $r-(K+m-1)/2<h_0$ and $m+2y\le(2-\beta)r$ with room for the rounding in Lemma 2.6; Lemma 5.1 and Lemma 5.3 use $T=\lceil \beta r\rceil +4$; Proposition 4.1 needs $T\ge\beta r+3$. We made no attempt to optimise the constant or the range $k\ge1000$. (All numerical inequalities of this section and of Section 5 were also checked by exact integer arithmetic for every $1000\le r\le 20000$; see Appendix A.)

## 7. Further structural lemmas (independent of Theorem 1.1)

The results of this section are not used in the proof of Theorem 1.1. They are tools toward the conjecture $f(k,7)=(3/4+o(1))k$. Here $\mathcal H$ is any family of finite nonempty sets (no uniformity) with property $(7,2)$ and $\tau(\mathcal H)\ge t$; thus every set of at most $t-1$ points is avoided by an edge. All of them rest on the following form of the Fano construction of [FKW].

**Lemma 7.1 (Fano labelling).** Let $\Pi$ be the Fano plane. Suppose edges $G_l$ are indexed by the seven lines $l$ of $\Pi$ (repetitions allowed) and there is a map $\pi$ from the vertex set to the points of $\Pi$ such that $v\in G_l$ implies $\pi(v)\notin l$. Then $\{G_l\}$ has no transversal of size at most two.

*Proof.* For vertices $v,w$ (possibly equal) choose a line $l$ through $\pi(v)$ and $\pi(w)$; then $v,w\notin G_l$.
 ∎

**Theorem 7.2 (span of good triples).** If $G_1,G_2,G_3\in\mathcal H$ satisfy $G_1\cap G_2\cap G_3=\emptyset$, then $|G_1\cup G_2\cup G_3|\ge2t-2$. Equivalently, if $\mathcal H$ has property $(7,2)$ and contains a good triple of union size $N$, then $\tau(\mathcal H)\le\lfloor N/2\rfloor +1$.

*Proof.* Let $U=G_1\cup G_2\cup G_3$, $N=|U|$, and suppose $N\le2t-3$. Label the Fano points $p_0,a,a',b,b',c,c'$ with lines $\{p_0,a,a'\}$, $\{p_0,b,b'\}$, $\{p_0,c,c'\}$ (the pencil through $p_0$) and $\{a,b,c\}$, $\{a',b',c\}$, $\{a',b,c'\}$, $\{a,b',c'\}$. Put $\mathcal A=U\setminus G_1$, $\mathcal B=G_1\setminus G_2$, $\mathcal C=G_1\cap G_2$ (a partition of $U$), and split $\mathcal A=\mathcal A_a\sqcup\mathcal A_{a'}$, $\mathcal B=\mathcal B_b\sqcup\mathcal B_{b'}$, $\mathcal C=\mathcal C_c\sqcup\mathcal C_{c'}$ as described below. Let $\pi$ map $\mathcal A_a$ to $a$, etc., and every vertex outside $U$ to $p_0$. Assign $G_1$ to $\{p_0,a,a'\}$ (it avoids $\mathcal A$ and lies in $U$), $G_2$ to $\{p_0,b,b'\}$ (it avoids $\mathcal B=G_1\setminus G_2$), and $G_3$ to $\{p_0,c,c'\}$ (it avoids $\mathcal C=G_1\cap G_2$ because the triple has no common point). For each of the four lines missing $p_0$, request an edge avoiding the union of its three classes. Then Lemma 7.1 applies: a vertex outside $U$ is labelled $p_0$, and the only lines through $p_0$ are the pencil lines, whose edges $G_1,G_2,G_3\subseteq U$ do not contain it; a vertex of $U$ labelled, say, $a$ lies in $\mathcal A$, hence not in $G_1$, and not in the two requested edges of the lines through $a$. We obtain a bad subfamily provided each of the four requested sets has at most $t-1$ points.

Each class occurs in exactly two of the four lines missing $p_0$, so the four loads sum to $2N$. Write $\epsilon_A=|\mathcal A_a|-|\mathcal A_{a'}|$, and similarly $\epsilon_B,\epsilon_C$; each can be chosen in $\{0\}$ (even class) or $\{\pm1\}$ (odd class). The loads equal $N/2+\tfrac12(\epsilon_A+\epsilon_B+\epsilon_C)$, $N/2+\tfrac12(-\epsilon_A-\epsilon_B+\epsilon_C)$, $N/2+\tfrac12(-\epsilon_A+\epsilon_B-\epsilon_C)$, $N/2+\tfrac12(\epsilon_A-\epsilon_B-\epsilon_C)$. With no odd class all loads are $N/2$; with one odd class they are $N/2\pm\frac12$; with two odd classes some choice gives loads in $\{N/2-1,N/2,N/2+1\}$; with three odd classes, all $\epsilon=-1$ gives loads $N/2-\tfrac32,N/2+\tfrac12,N/2+\tfrac12,N/2+\tfrac12$. In every case the maximum load is at most $\lfloor N/2\rfloor +1\le t-1$ when $N\le2t-3$. So each request is legal, giving a bad subfamily of seven edges, a contradiction.
 ∎

**Remark 7.3.** Theorem 7.2 is sharp for the complete hypergraph $K^{(5)}_9$, which has property $(7,2)$: seven $5$-subsets of a $9$-set without a $2$-point transversal would have complements forming seven $4$-sets that cover all pairs of the $9$ points, but the covering number $C(9,4,2)$ equals $8>7$ (checked by an exact integer program; see Appendix A). Hence then $t=\tau(K^{(5)}_9)=5$, and $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$, $\{1,2,6,7,8\}$, $\{3,4,6,7,8\}$ is a good triple of union size $8=2t-2$. The parity choice of the splits is what gives $2t-2$.

**Theorem 7.4 (two-colour lemma).** Let $E_0,b_1,b_2,c_1,c_2\in\mathcal H$ with $b_1\cap b_2\cap E_0=\emptyset=c_1\cap c_2\cap E_0$, and let $E_0=D_A\sqcup D_B$ be a partition with

$$
E_0\cap\bigl((b_1\cap c_1)\cup(b_2\cap c_2)\bigr)\subseteq D_A,\qquad E_0\cap\bigl((b_1\cap c_2)\cup(b_2\cap c_1)\bigr)\subseteq D_B .
$$

Then at least one of

$$
T_A=D_A\cup(b_1\cap c_1)\cup(b_2\cap c_2),\qquad T_B=D_B\cup(b_1\cap c_2)\cup(b_2\cap c_1)
$$

is a transversal of $\mathcal H$.

*Proof.* Suppose not, and let $g_1,g_2\in\mathcal H$ avoid $T_A$, $T_B$ respectively. Label the Fano points $p_0,p_1,q,r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4$ with lines

$$
\begin{gathered}
L=\{p_0,p_1,q\},\quad B_1=\{p_0,r_1,r_2\},\quad B_2=\{p_0,r_3,r_4\},\quad C_1=\{p_1,r_1,r_3\},\\ C_2=\{p_1,r_2,r_4\},\quad M_1=\{q,r_1,r_4\},\quad M_2=\{q,r_2,r_3\},
\end{gathered}
$$

and assign $E_0,b_1,b_2,c_1,c_2,g_1,g_2$ to $L,B_1,B_2,C_1,C_2,M_1,M_2$. We define $\pi$ so that $v\in G_l\Rightarrow\pi(v)\notin l$, and apply Lemma 7.1.

*Vertices of $E_0$.* A vertex of $D_A$ gets $r_1$ or $r_4$ (points of $M_1$; $g_1$ misses $D_A\subseteq T_A$). The label $r_1$ is forbidden only if $v\in b_1\cup c_1$ and $r_4$ only if $v\in b_2\cup c_2$; both are forbidden only if $v\in(b_1\cap c_2)\cup(b_2\cap c_1)$ (recall $v$ is not in both $b$'s nor both $c$'s), which is impossible for $v\in D_A$. Symmetrically a vertex of $D_B$ gets $r_2$ or $r_3$ ($r_2$ forbidden by $b_1\cup c_2$, $r_3$ by $b_2\cup c_1$), which is possible since $v\notin(b_1\cap c_1)\cup(b_2\cap c_2)$, and $g_2$ misses $D_B$.

*Vertices outside $E_0$.* If $v\notin b_1\cup b_2$ put $\pi(v)=p_0$ (lines $L,B_1,B_2$); if $v\notin c_1\cup c_2$ put $\pi(v)=p_1$ (lines $L,C_1,C_2$). Otherwise $v$ lies in one of $b_1\cap c_1$, $b_2\cap c_2$ (subsets of $T_A$) or $b_1\cap c_2$, $b_2\cap c_1$ (subsets of $T_B$). Take $v\in b_1\cap c_1$; then $v\notin g_1$. If $v\notin g_2$ put $\pi(v)=q$ (lines $L,M_1,M_2$). If $v\in g_2$ then $v\notin T_B$, so $v\notin c_2$ and $v\notin b_2$; the lines containing $v$'s edges are among $B_1,C_1,M_2$, whose union misses $r_4$; put $\pi(v)=r_4$. The other three cases are identical: $v\in b_2\cap c_2$, $v\in g_2$ gives lines among $B_2,C_2,M_2$, missing $r_1$; $v\in b_1\cap c_2$, $v\in g_1$ gives lines among $B_1,C_2,M_1$, missing $r_3$; $v\in b_2\cap c_1$, $v\in g_1$ gives lines among $B_2,C_1,M_1$, missing $r_2$.

By Lemma 7.1 the seven edges form a bad subfamily, contradicting property $(7,2)$.
 ∎

**Theorem 7.5 ($K_4$ criterion).** Let $E_0\in\mathcal H$. Suppose $E_0=E_1\sqcup E_2\sqcup E_3\sqcup E_4$ and there are six edges $G_{ab}$ ($1\le a<b\le4$) with $G_{ab}\cap E_0\subseteq E_a\cup E_b$ such that no vertex outside $E_0$ lies in $G_{ab}\cap G_{bc}\cap G_{ac}$ for any three distinct $a,b,c$. Then $\{E_0\}\cup\{G_{ab}\}$ is a bad subfamily. Conversely, every seven edges indexed by Fano lines and admitting a labelling as in Lemma 7.1, one of which is $E_0$, arise in this way.

*Proof.* Take a line $L=\{s_1,s_2,s_3\}$ and the four points $r_1,\dots,r_4$ off $L$. Each of the six other lines contains exactly one $s_i$ and two points $r_c,r_d$; assign to it the edge $G_{ab}$, $\{a,b\}=[4]\setminus\{c,d\}$, and assign $E_0$ to $L$. Label $v\in E_a$ by $r_a$: the lines through $r_a$ other than $L$ carry $G_{bc},G_{bd},G_{cd}$ with $\{b,c,d\}=[4]\setminus\{a\}$, whose traces on $E_0$ avoid $E_a$. For $v\notin E_0$ let $\sigma(v)$ be the set of pairs $ab$ with $v\in G_{ab}$, viewed as edges of $K_4$. The lines through $s_i$ carry the edges of a perfect matching of $K_4$, and the lines through $r_a$ (other than $L$) carry the triangle on $[4]\setminus\{a\}$. So $v$ can be labelled iff $\sigma(v)$ is disjoint from some perfect matching or from some triangle. If $\sigma(v)$ meets all three perfect matchings, it contains three edges, one from each matching, and such a triple is either a triangle or a star; a triangle-free $\sigma(v)$ meeting all matchings contains a star $\{ab,ac,ad\}$ and no further edge (adding any edge creates a triangle), hence it is disjoint from the triangle on $\{b,c,d\}$. Thus $v$ can be labelled whenever $\sigma(v)$ contains no triangle, which is the hypothesis. Lemma 7.1 gives the first claim. Conversely, given such a labelled Fano tuple with $E_0$ on $L$, the vertices of $E_0$ carry labels off $L$; let $E_a$ be those labelled $r_a$, and the same dictionary shows the trace condition, while a vertex outside $E_0$ lying in a triangle $G_{ab}\cap G_{bc}\cap G_{ac}$ would meet all matchings and all triangles and could not be labelled.
 ∎

**Theorem 7.6 (spread lemma).** Let $E_0\in\mathcal H$ and $E_0=E_1\sqcup E_2\sqcup E_3\sqcup E_4$, and put $s=t-1-\max(|E_1\cup E_4|,|E_2\cup E_3|)\ge0$. Let $b_1,b_2\in\mathcal H$ with $b_1\cap E_0\subseteq E_3\cup E_4$ and $b_2\cap E_0\subseteq E_1\cup E_2$. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability distributions on $\mathcal O_{24}=\{G\in\mathcal H:G\cap E_0\subseteq E_2\cup E_4\}$ and $\mathcal O_{13}=\{G\in\mathcal H:G\cap E_0\subseteq E_1\cup E_3\}$, and let $p=\max_{v\notin E_0}\mu(G\ni v)$, $q=\max_{v\notin E_0}\nu(G\ni v)$. Then

$$
|(b_1\cup b_2)\setminus E_0|\,(p+q)\ \ge\ s+1 .
$$

In particular, if $\mathcal H$ has rank at most $k$ and the partition is balanced ($|E_1\cup E_4|=\lceil |E_0|/2\rceil $, $|E_2\cup E_3|=\lfloor |E_0|/2\rfloor $), then $t\le\lceil |E_0|/2\rceil +2k(p+q)$; if moreover $p,q\le1/16$ then $t\le\lceil k/2\rceil +k/4$.

*Proof.* For $c_1\in\mathcal O_{24}$ and $c_2\in\mathcal O_{13}$ apply Theorem 7.4 with $D_A=E_1\cup E_4$, $D_B=E_2\cup E_3$: the hypotheses hold since $b_1\cap b_2\cap E_0=\emptyset=c_1\cap c_2\cap E_0$, $b_1\cap c_1\cap E_0\subseteq E_4$, $b_2\cap c_2\cap E_0\subseteq E_1$, $b_1\cap c_2\cap E_0\subseteq E_3$ and $b_2\cap c_1\cap E_0\subseteq E_2$. So $T_A$ or $T_B$ is a transversal and has at least $t$ points. Both are contained in $D_A\cup W$, resp. $D_B\cup W$, where $W=((b_1\cup b_2)\cap(c_1\cup c_2))\setminus E_0$; hence $|W|\ge s+1$ for every such $c_1,c_2$. Draw $c_1\sim\mu$ and $c_2\sim\nu$ independently. Then

$$
s+1\le\mathbb E|W|\le\sum_{v\in(b_1\cup b_2)\setminus E_0}\bigl(\Pr[v\in c_1]+\Pr[v\in c_2]\bigr)\le|(b_1\cup b_2)\setminus E_0|(p+q).
$$

For the consequences use $|(b_1\cup b_2)\setminus E_0|\le2k$ and $s+1=t-\lceil |E_0|/2\rceil $ (if $s<0$ the bound $t\le\lceil |E_0|/2\rceil $ is immediate).
 ∎

**Remark 7.7.** Theorems 7.4--7.6 only produce bad subfamilies of *Fano type* (Lemma 7.1). By an example in the working note (two disjoint parts, coefficient approaching $4/5$ in a continuous type model), Fano-type tuples alone cannot handle families with disjoint edges; any proof of the $3/4$ bound along these lines must also use other bad seven-tuples. Theorem 7.6 shows that in a hypothetical family with $t\ge(3/4+\varepsilon)k$ and rank $k$, for every edge and every balanced quartering, the two "outside clouds" cannot both be $\tfrac1{16}$-spread.

## 8. Concluding remarks

The chain of Section 6 cannot be pushed much further with the same ingredients: a numerical optimisation (mixed-integer programming over four-request static label templates, not a proof) suggests that the best static budget at the binding configuration of the local proposition is about $0.862r$, so new adaptive ideas are needed below roughly $0.862$ [numerical observation only]. The unpublished, computer-assisted route mentioned in Remark 1.3 reaches $6/7$. The conjecture $f(k,7)=(3/4+o(1))k$ remains open.

## Appendix A. Independent computer checks (sanity supplement)

The proof above does not depend on any computation. The following exact checks were run as independent confirmation; all use exact rational or integer arithmetic.
1. `w5_paper_prop10_vertices.py` (written for this manuscript, independent of earlier scripts): enumerates the vertices of the closure of each of the nine case polytopes of Proposition 4.1 (a, b1, b2, b3, c1, c2, c3, c4 split A, c4 split B) and checks, at every vertex, every lemma hypothesis as stated in Section 3 and every auxiliary inequality asserted in the text, including (C), $(*)$ and the condition (ii) of case (c2). Since each hypothesis is a convex piecewise-linear function bounded by a constant (or affine on each split branch), vertex checks cover the polytopes. Result: all pass; every case polytope is nonempty (a: 4, b1: 14, b2: 10, b3: 4, c1: 6, c2: 5, c3: 6, c4A: 6, c4B: 6 vertices); a randomised exact test finds no point of the region outside the union of the case polytopes. A mutation (budget $0.8645$) produces failures.
2. `w5_paper_constants.py`: checks with exact integers every numerical inequality of Section 6, Lemma 5.1, Lemma 5.3 (at $\beta'=\beta$) and the budget of Lemma 3.1 at $m=\lfloor 119r/400\rfloor $, for every $r$ with $1000\le r\le20000$ (and in fact $80\le r\le 20000$). Result: all pass.
3. Referee scripts from an earlier review round (same directory): `referee_w4_handbound_vertices.py` (vertex enumeration of the case polytopes), `referee_w4_handbound_fm.py` (Fourier--Motzkin elimination with strictness flags, showing each case system together with the negation of each lemma inequality is infeasible), `referee_w4_handbound_int.py` (exhaustive integer check of Proposition 4.1 with $T=\lceil \beta r\rceil +3$ and the rounded S1 splits: $9{,}980{,}329$ triples at $r=1000$ and all triples at several smaller $r$, no failure), `referee_w4_handbound_indep.py`, `referee_w4_handbound_s1s2.py`, `referee_w4_handbound_static_indep.py` (explicit set systems: every candidate pair of S1 and S2 is covered and all request sizes are at most $T$; the S1 closed form agrees with the exact linear-programming optimum), and `referee_w4_handbound_exh.py` (for all $r\le12$, an exhaustive first-response adversary for Lemmas 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 with exact treatment of the final responses; no failure, while the mutation $T-1$ fails).

For this manuscript we re-ran `referee_w4_handbound_vertices.py`, `referee_w4_handbound_fm.py` and `referee_w4_handbound_int.py` (the latter at $r=200,333,401$ and exhaustively at $r=1000$, $9{,}980{,}329$ triples); all pass. The remaining scripts of item 3 were run in the earlier review round and were not re-run here. All these checks confirm arithmetic and case coverage only; the mathematical content is in the proofs.
